text: This is a DOS Doom port on a Sega Saturn, captured on real hardware.
Can it run it? Let's see that together.
Welcome to the first devlog episode.
The walls are drawn by one chip, and almost everything else by another.
Nothing here was built initially for the Saturn -- the WAD content is read off the disc as it is.
Eight to fifteen frames per second, on average, across these three clips.
But this episode is about something else: chip synchronisation.
Standing still, the picture is fine. It only tears when it moves.
Walking forward, one frame of lateness moves the picture by a few pixels.
But turning around? it moves it by the rotation angle.
Watch these three frames. The room moves, and the walls stay. Then the walls move, and the room stays.
Each layer moves in exactly the frame the other one does not.
The weapon and the status bar are drawn by VDP1 as well, and they are just as late.
Nothing is wrong with either of them, because neither one moves with the room.
Same chip, same frame, same lateness. It only breaks where the content follows the world.
These are two hardware captures, one month apart.
Whether the drawing was finished was read from a flag called CEF.
And the manual says that flag is reset by the very swap it is supposed to gate.
On real hardware, it latches on about half the frames.
The manual gets two things wrong on the same page, on the same developer CD.
With the word frame, the sentence means nothing. With the word field, it is an instruction.
And the register value it prescribes is the one that means: stay automatic.
The sequence that works is the one SEGA's own library shipped, and Lobotomy shipped in Quake.
In split screen, when the queue runs short, the walls now give up their place to the monsters.
